title: The shepherd
hook: he tends sheep for pay, and later says every prophet was a shepherd (Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abu Talib's house. Your line was: there was room. Where did you make room for one more? Day seven hundred twelve.

Arak berries, small and dark, picked off the bush by a group of men on the road. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is with them, a grown man now, and he tells them: pick the black ones, they're the best. Someone asks him a question about that. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps the question, and his answer opens a door onto the hills outside Mecca and a young man with a stick and a flock. Today: the shepherd.
screen: `ARAK BERRIES BY THE ROAD.` → `"PICK THE BLACK ONES."` → `A QUESTION.`

segments.voice: The companions ask: were you a shepherd? And in al-Bukhari's report he answers with a question of his own: is there any prophet who was not? In another report in al-Bukhari, he says it plainly. Allah sent no prophet who did not tend sheep. They ask: and you? Yes, he says. I tended them for the people of Mecca, for a few coins. So the orphan from Abu Talib's crowded house earned his keep in the hills, walking slowly behind other people's animals. The Qur'an knows this work. In surah twenty, Allah asks Musa what is in his right hand, and Musa answers, in Pickthall's words: "This is my staff whereon I lean, and wherewith I beat down branches for my sheep, and wherein I find other uses." A man about to be sent to Pharaoh, and his first answer is about sheep. Why would shepherding come before prophethood? The hadith doesn't explain, and it's fair to leave that open. Commentators have offered reasons: sheep are slow and they scatter, and a shepherd learns patience, watchfulness, and how to bring back the one that wanders. Whatever the reason, the Prophet carried the word into his teaching. In al-Bukhari he says: each of you is a shepherd, and each of you is responsible for his flock. The ruler, the parent, the worker with someone else's property. In Arabic, a shepherd is ra'i, and the flock is ra'iyyah, from the same root. Everyone, in that saying, is watching over something.
screen: `"IS THERE A PROPHET WHO WAS NOT?"` · `FOR THE PEOPLE OF MECCA, FOR COINS.` · `MUSA'S STAFF, FOR HIS SHEEP.` · `EACH OF YOU IS A SHEPHERD.` · then, large: `EVERY PROPHET WAS A SHEPHERD.`

segments.voice: The practice: care for something small and slow. Settle, and breathe. What's in your keeping that moves at its own pace? A plant, a pet, an old parent, a child learning to read, a project that won't be rushed. Bring it to mind, and match its speed. Don't hurry it in your head. Watch it the way a shepherd watches a flock, noticing which part is wandering off. What would bringing it back gently look like today? If you pray, you can ask Allah for a shepherd's patience. If not, just stay slow with it. The bell holds the time.
The shepherd. The Prophet tended sheep for the people of Mecca, and said in al-Bukhari that Allah sent no prophet who did not. Today's word.
Your line: every prophet was a shepherd. Today, give one slow thing in your care ten unhurried minutes: water it, walk it, sit with it, read with it. Day seven hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Muslims quote the hadith 'each of you is a shepherd, and each of you is responsible for his flock' when speaking of responsibility in families, work and leadership.

fork.setup: the Prophet ﷺ tells the companions to pick the black arak berries. they ask: were you a shepherd? what does he answer?

is there any prophet who was not a shepherd?

fork.reveal: al-Bukhari reports his answer as a question: is there any prophet who did not tend sheep?

original.note: Arabic: ra'i, shepherd; the flock in the hadith is ra'iyyah, from the same root.

trapdoor: what you thought: a boy's summer job.
what it means: every prophet tended sheep, and every person is a shepherd of something.
what a scholar hears: al-Bukhari on prophets as shepherds, Musa's staff in 20:18, and ra'i / ra'iyyah in 'each of you is a shepherd.'
